analysis.one_liner: Bars giant online platforms from favoring their own products over rivals' on their services.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite bipartisan sponsorship from nine senators including the Judiciary chair and the panel's top Republican.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for the largest online platforms to use their market power against the businesses and users that depend on them. Platforms could no longer rig search results or app stores in favor of their own products, use data gathered from business users to build competing products, block companies from accessing their own data, or make it hard to uninstall preinstalled apps. The FTC, the Justice Department, and state attorneys general could sue, with penalties up to 10% of a company's U.S. revenue.
analysis.who_benefits: Small businesses, app developers, and third-party sellers who sell through big platforms, and the consumers who use those platforms. Businesses would compete on the merits instead of losing placement to the platform's own products, consumers would keep more choice and control over defaults and preinstalled software, and the bill explicitly protects users who report violations from retaliation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small sellers, app makers, and platform users

how_it_helps.text: Platforms could not preference their own products, services, or lines of business over those of other business users in ways that materially harm competition.
Platforms could not use nonpublic data generated by business users on the platform to build competing products, and could not block business users from taking their own data elsewhere.
Platforms could not restrict users from uninstalling preinstalled apps or changing default settings that steer them to the platform's own products, except for security needs.

The FTC, Justice Department, and state attorneys general could sue violators in federal court, with civil penalties up to 10% of the company's total U.S. revenue; courts could also order corporate officers to forfeit compensation for repeat violations.
Platforms could not retaliate against users or business users who report suspected violations to law enforcement in good faith.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of giant platform companies — the bill's thresholds would capture platforms with 50 million or more U.S. monthly users whose owners have roughly $550 billion in sales or market value — which would face litigation risk, compliance costs, and penalties, and potentially give up revenue from self-preferencing. Some platform features and integrations could be harder to offer.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued the rules are drawn broadly enough to cover legitimate platform management, forcing years of litigation over everyday decisions about search ranking, app store rules, and product design.

Critics warned that requirements to share data and interoperability could create real privacy and security risks; the bill responds with affirmative defenses for safety, privacy, and security, but places the burden on the platform to prove its conduct was necessary.

Compliance and litigation costs would be substantial for covered companies, and some costs could ultimately be passed on to users or advertisers, though the bill's competition rules aim to counteract that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a specific, concentrated problem: a few companies acting as both marketplace and competitor. The restrictions are limited to the very largest platforms, and the bill built in defenses for security, privacy, and core functionality, plus carve-outs for intellectual property, encryption, and foreign adversaries. The main honest cost is litigation uncertainty for the covered companies and possibly higher operating costs; the main gain is a fairer deal for the millions of small businesses and consumers who use those platforms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never held a markup or vote on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on June 15, 2023, joined by eight cosponsors spanning both parties: Sens. Grassley, Durbin, Graham, Blumenthal, Hawley, Hirono, Warner, and Booker.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on June 15, 2023; no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever taken.
The committee's chair, Sen. Durbin, was himself an original cosponsor, yet the committee never scheduled a markup during the two-year Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large platform companies the bill would have regulated, whose shareholders avoided new competition rules, litigation risk, and penalties that could reach 10% of U.S. revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The giant platforms the bill would have regulated

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized a bipartisan group of eight cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (IA), former Judiciary chairman and ranking member
for.what_they_did: Original Republican cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan standing on the committee that would handle it.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but his committee never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

for.name: 6 additional Democratic and 3 additional Republican senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill: Sens. Blumenthal, Hirono, Warner, and Booker (D); Sens. Graham, Hawley, and one more (R).

against.name: Google, Amazon, Apple, and Meta
against.role: Covered platform companies and the main lobbying force against it
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against the antitrust package, which was the most direct regulatory threat to their business models.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, and it never advanced out of committee either.

sides.party_line_note: Support split both parties: 5 of 48 Senate Democrats and 3 of 49 Senate Republicans cosponsored, and the bill still never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.industry: Large tech platform companies (search, app stores, e-commerce, social media)
industries.note: The bill would have made it unlawful for these companies to self-preference, exploit business-user data, and lock in defaults, with penalties up to 10% of U.S. revenue. Their interest in the bill ran against consumers and the small businesses that depend on their marketplaces.

industries.industry: Small businesses, app developers, and third-party sellers on major platforms
industries.note: These businesses would compete on the merits instead of against the platform's own products, could carry their customer data to other services, and could not be retaliated against for reporting violations. Their gain is the same as the public's: lower prices and more choice.
